answer: LINE (Large-scale Information Network Embedding) uses the alias table method to make edge sampling in its edge-sampling treatment efficient. The core idea is to preprocess the discrete edge distribution once, building an alias table that stores, for each edge, a small amount of auxiliary information so that a sample can later be drawn in constant time. After this preprocessing, each sampled edge is obtained by two O(1) operations: one uniform random index lookup into the table and one constant-time accept/reject decision using the stored probability threshold. As a result, the per-sample cost of edge sampling is O(1), while the one-time table construction cost is paid upfront. In LINE, this matters because the method is designed to learn local and global network structure from large graphs, so reducing training time complexity is important for scalability. More generally, the alias table method is a standard constant-time discrete sampling technique, and LINE applies it to edge sampling rather than to random walks or neighborhood sampling.
